title: Why reading to a dog helps shy readers (and how to try it at home)
excerpt: Libraries are inviting children to read aloud to calm therapy dogs, and research suggests the gentle audience can lift confidence. Here's how to borrow the idea at home, with or without a pet.

body.p: Last week a Florida library system made local news for a simple idea: children reading picture books aloud to a dog. The Alachua County Library District runs a Read With a Dog programme in which elementary-aged children sit beside a certified therapy dog and read to it. Librarians and parents told WUFT News they have seen children grow more confident.

Why a dog? A dog never corrects a mispronounced word, never sighs and never looks at the clock. For a child who is still sounding out words, that patient, non-judging listener can take the pressure off.

The evidence is encouraging but still small. A 2022 study in the Early Childhood Education Journal followed 24 Canadian children aged about 7 to 8 who needed extra reading support. Each child spent eight weeks reading to a dog and eight weeks reading to an adult, about 15 minutes a week. Oral reading and comprehension improved in both programmes, so the dog was not magic. But the children were noticeably more enthusiastic about the dog sessions, and only the dog sessions were described as calm. Parents and teachers saw better attitudes to reading after both.

An earlier UC Davis project found similar gains in reading fluency among children who read to rescue dogs each week. Even so, researchers are careful: a reading dog builds comfort and motivation, while skills still come from teaching and practice.

body.h: How to bring the idea home

ul: Ask your local library whether it hosts a reading-dog session.
If you have a calm family pet, invite your child to read a short book to it. Five to ten minutes is plenty.
No pet? A favourite stuffed animal works too. Let your child be the teacher who shows the pictures and reads the story.
Choose easy, familiar books for these sessions. The goal is fluency and fun, not a challenge.
Stay nearby but quiet. Resist correcting every slip; praise the effort afterwards.
Younger children (3 to 5) can 'read' by retelling a story from the pictures. That counts too.

body.tip: Tonight, set out a cushion, a teddy or the family dog, and a book your child already knows well. Ask: Can you read this one to Teddy? Then just listen.

title: Cozy picture books are topping the 2026 holiday gift lists
excerpt: The season's gift guides are full of warm, funny picture books. Here's what's getting attention, and a simple way to pick the right book for the child on your list.

body.p: Gift-guide season has arrived, and this year the children's lists lean cozy. The Associated Press holiday roundup mixes snug board books with a few delightfully spooky reads, and one title that keeps coming up is Your Truck by Jon Klassen, published by Candlewick Press. Klassen's dry humour and quiet pictures have made him a favourite with parents who read the same book forty nights in a row.

November also brought a strong crop of new releases. Book Riot's monthly roundup highlights Good Bear, Bad Bear by Hyewon Yum, out November 3: a little girl decides that if her sister is always the good one, she must be the bad one. It is a gentle doorway into a feeling many siblings know well. And for early readers who love comics, the newest Dog Man by Dav Pilkey is the most anticipated children's book of the month.

Award season is underway too. The New York Times and New York Public Library have named their ten Best Illustrated Children's Books of 2026, a list worth browsing if you want a book that will also look beautiful on the shelf.

body.h: How to choose a picture book gift

ul: Ages 0–2: sturdy board books with bold pictures, rhythm and repetition.
Ages 3–5: a story with a clear feeling at its heart (fear of the dark, a new sibling, sharing) and pictures that reward a second look.
Ages 6–8: longer read-alouds, funny early chapter books and comics that build confidence.
Any age: think about what the child already loves (trucks, animals, space) and start there.

body.tip: Write a short message on the first page before you wrap it. A dated inscription turns a book into a keepsake a child will find again years later.

title: Learning to read vs. choosing to read: why the bedtime story still matters
excerpt: A 2026 publishing report warns that a heavy focus on literacy skills can crowd out the joy of reading. A calm bedtime routine is one of the easiest fixes.

body.p: Every year, HarperCollins Children's Books and Farshore publish a review of children's reading for pleasure. The 2026 edition, built on NielsenIQ data and research with The Reading Agency, carries a pointed theme: there is a difference between a child who can read and a child who chooses to.

The report's argument is that literacy can be taught and tested, while the love of reading has to be encouraged, modelled and kept free of pressure. When reading at home starts to feel like more homework, some children quietly stop picking up books on their own. Its practical answer is a regular reading routine: a predictable, relaxed moment with a book that children come to look forward to.

That matters because shared reading has been slipping. An Education Week report in 2025 found that only about a third of parents of five- to seven-year-olds said they regularly read to their children.

body.h: Five ways to make bedtime reading feel like a treat

ul: Let your child choose the book, even if it's the same one every night.
Keep it short. Ten unhurried minutes beat a rushed half hour.
Do the voices. Children remember the silly ones for years.
Talk about the pictures and ask what they think happens next.
Never use reading as a punishment or a chore to tick off.

body.tip: Dim the lights, put the phones in another room and end with the same closing words each night. The ritual itself tells a child's body it is time to rest.

title: Kids' reading for fun is rising again. Here's how to keep it going at home
excerpt: After a 20-year low, children's enjoyment of reading has ticked up for the first time in five years. But young boys are moving the other way.

body.p: There is some good news for families who love books. The National Literacy Trust's 2026 Annual Literacy Survey, answered by more than 125,000 children and young people across the UK aged 5 to 18, found that reading enjoyment and daily reading have risen for the first time in five years, after hitting a 20-year low in 2025.

The lift is modest. Just over one in three children aged 8 to 18 (36.1%) said they enjoyed reading. Among the youngest readers, aged 5 to 8, enjoyment is still high at 61.6%, but it slipped slightly from the year before, and the drop came from boys. The survey also found the gap between children from lower-income families and their peers is widening.
The Trust's main lesson is simple: children read more in their free time when books connect to what they already care about.

ul: Follow their interests: dinosaurs, football, space, animals. Any topic is a way in.
Count everything: comics, joke books, recipes and magazines are all real reading.
Keep books within reach, in the car, by the bed, next to the sofa.
Let them see you reading. Children copy what we do far more than what we say.
For boys aged 5 to 8 especially, try funny books, comics and stories full of action.

body.tip: Visit the library together once a month and let your child choose freely. Owning the choice is half the fun.
